doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Nussbaum's parents and becoming a musician
summary: Nussbaum's artist parents wanted him prepared; he left Emerson, became a working musician, and describes the cost of life on the road.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Right. You said you came from an artistic family. Did you get any — can I assume you got encouragement?

Yes I did. My parents both were very pragmatic in the regard to my father was a fine artist. He never made his living as an artist. He made his living doing technical illustration so he still utilized his craft but not to the sense of expression that he was able to do. And my mother had been involved with acting and then she got involved, because of her aesthetic viewpoint, got involved with graphic design and advertising. So both of them didn’t really make their living at what their passion was. So they were both very concerned because of what their reality had been, with me being properly prepared to have something to fall back on. So consequently they said look, I mean originally I went to school at Emerson College for one year to study liberal arts. But I was getting so into playing, I said what am I doing, I might as well put my focus in more towards the music. They just wanted me to be prepared for the tactics of this world we live in. But I think that — I never finished school, I just started getting out there and playing. So I mean I know that I gave them a great amount of satisfaction knowing that I have been somehow able to eke out a living playing music. And it’s not easy. I mean I’m traveling all the time because I just can’t stay home and do it. It’s kind of like a blessing and a curse. I mean the blessing is being able to go out and play music with great people. Every night is an adventure. You never know what’s going to happen. The curse is I have to be away from my family a lot, got a lot of miles on me, can’t stay home on a regular basis, but I don’t think I could do anything else. It’s kind of like I need it. And I don’t think I made a conscious decision to become a musician. It was just, it just kind of happened. You know I loved doing it, people call you, they get your number, you go to the gig, you get another gig. You know it just seemed to happen that way and if you are really trying to think intelligently and realistically, man, go out and get a job where you know you can make a

steady check. If a young person is debating in their mind, well should I go for the security or should I go out and try it, well you know if you’re having to think about it then maybe you’re not supposed to be doing it. I mean with me I just kind of look at it as though this kind of happened. I guess it kind of picked me. And I had to go with it, so I did. And I mean if you’re young and you’re not sure about it and you have no responsibilities and you can just go out there and give it a shot, give it a shot. Try. See what’s going to happen. Once you have the realities of marriage, mortgage, children, all that, you may not have that opportunity to give it a shot.
